New to Voat and wanted to post one of my favorite interviews! Kurt Russell is my favorite actor. This is part of an interview he did with Jeff Wells of Hollywood-Elsewhere during a Hateful Eight press circuit. This snippet is the last part of the interview, when Wells decided to turn the discussion to violence in film and then to gun control and Kurt Russell was having none of it.

Here is the transcript of this last segment of the interview and the link to their article if you're interested: http://www.hollywood-elsewhere.com/2015/12/mild-mannered-wells-vs-irked-russell-on-terrorists-san-bernardino-gun-culture-gun-controls-etc/

Wells: The Quentin cult, if you will, is, like, 23 years old, starting with Reservoir Dogs…right? Violence as attitude, violence as style, violence as fashion…not dealt with in an earnest, realistic way. The swagger thing.

Russell: Right.

Wells: And I was looking in the N.Y. Times this morning and this guy interviewed several people in the country in the Midwest and West. And with almost everybody out there, he reported, there’s a feeling of anxiety in the culture…when’s the next one?

Russell: So how do you connect the dots?

Wells: I think there’s a feeling about shootings and violence right now…I think it’s different in 2015 than it was in the mid ’90s. But Quentin is still playing the same game more or less.

Russell: Well, Quentin does what he does. He’s painting a picture, writing, telling a story…like a filmmaker. But to mix and match reality with fantasy is something I don’t understand but that’s just me. I think we should understand the difference. To mix today’s politics with, in this case, a tale about, uh, a fictional tale about the Civil War…

Wells: I’m not talking about politics. I’m talking about a ground-level, water-table…a feeling in people’s bones. People are genuinely…between Paris and San Bernardino the idea of sudden violence becoming a normal, day-to-day aspect coming from the gun culture and everything else…it’s a different vibe, you know?

Russell: I don’t understand concepts of conversation [about] the gun culture. We’ve lived with guns since, what, the 7th Century or something? I don’t know.

Wells: Well, I think we all know…guns are a trope. Not a trope but a totem, a metaphor that disenfranchised white guys need…it makes them feel good about themselves.

Russell: You can say what you want. I don’t agree with that. It’s not my thing.

Wells: Well, it’s statistically irrefutable.

Russell: If you think gun control is going to change the terrorists’ point of view, I think you’re, like, out of your mind. I think anybody [who says that] is. I think it’s absolutely insane. The problem, the problem that we’re having right now to turn it around…you may think you’ve got me worried about you’re gonna do? Dude, you’re about to find out what I’m gonna do, and that’s gonna worry you a lot more. And that‘s what we need. That will change the concept of gun culture, as you call it, to something [like] reality. Which is, if I’m a hockey team and I’ve got some guy bearing down on me as a goal tender, I’m not concerned about what he’s gonna do — I’m gonna make him concerned about what I’m gonna do…

Wells: I get that.

Russell: To stop him. That‘s when things change. [Tries to steer conversation back to the usual-usual, western genre, what Quentin does, asking the question, themes explored.] So what has that got to do with movies? Nothing! Movies are movies. They’re like a painting, like a song, like a book…he’s doing his Quentin Tarantino world, which I think belongs on film. I don’t think it has anything to do with anything outside of film. The music, the manipulation of the screenplay. So I can’t connect the dots. It really is hard for me to connect the dots.

Wells: Obama’s point was that the guys on the no-fly list, [there] for good reason because of terrorist connections or suspicions…they can get hold of a gun pretty easily.

Russell: They can also make a bomb pretty easily. So what? They can also get knives and stab you. Whaddaya gonna do about that? They can also get cars and run you over. Whaddaya gonna do about that?

Wells: They didn’t kill the people in San Bernardino with cars.

Russell: But they’ve killed others that way, haven’t they? Yeah, yeah. Whaddaya gonna do? Outlaw everything? That isn’t the answer.

Wells: Just put some controls…

Russell: Put some controls? What, so the people, so the people who want to defend themselves can’t?

Wells: No, not so you can’t, just so the idiots can’t get hold of them [so easily], that’s all.

Russell: You really believe they’re not going to? Are you serious about that? What good will that…? Oh my God. You and I just disagree.

Wells: Okay.

Russell: You and I just disagree. I understand that you think you can control the behavior of people that are dead set on taking your way of life away from you. You think you can control that? And there’s only one thing you can do with that. And that’s [to say} ‘No, dude, that’s not gonna happen. That’s just not gonna happen.’

My time as a recruiter was a shitshow, so this will be a part 1 post.

Now on recruiting duty, they don't really care what you do, what laws you break, what regulations you violate, or who you fuck. Basically, all you had to do was put people in the Army, pay your government credit card bill, and never get caught. There was no doubt in my mind that my company leadership knew that I would go above and beyond what is morally or legally right to put people in the Army, they just didn't want to know about it. Transgender people joined the Army through our company, long before the "don't ask don't tell" was repealed.

Recruiting duty was hell. I'd rather do 2-3 back to back deployments than a year on recruiting. I even bought a shotgun with the intent of blowing my brains out, and would sit there some nights with it on the coffee table, hoping that I would be able to drink up the courage to finally pull the trigger before I passed out. Look up recruiter suicides if you don't believe me. There's different types of stress, and the stress of war, I could deal with, this type of stress, I was at my breaking point.

This story is about "George", and the lengths I went through to get him in the Army.

"Have you ever thought about joining the Army?" - I said this so many times a day that I was saying it on my sleep. I see these two teenagers walking out of this fast food joint, applications in hand, and I gave them my one liner.

"Fuck you!"

"Ok, well if you ever want a real job, here's my card."

They threw it away in front of me. Rejection is all part of the game. They love to crunch the numbers. For how ever many people got talk to, you'll get rejected; for how ever many people that do sit down and hear you out, so many will go take the ASVAB and medical; and for however many people are actually qualified, so many will join.

Maybe a week or two later, I'm returning to the recruiting station, and these same two gentlemen are sitting at my desk. They didn't get the job at the fast food joint. No education, not even a GED, but not disqualifying law violations, yet....

At the time, the Army was offering to pay for GED classes and enlist on the condition that they had their GED by their ship out date. They didn't need the payment because the schools offered free GED classes for people under 21. I took them down, got them enrolled, and got them off drugs.... Well, let's just say that I made sure they would pass the drug test. No one I sent down to MEPS failed a drug test.

This story isn't about "Raphael", because Raphael was a model fucking DEP, actually quit using drugs, studied his ass off, came to the DEP training, and talked two more people into enlisting in the Army too. No complaints about Raphael.

George, on the other hand, I never heard from after he signed his enlistment paperwork unless I was at his doorstep waking his ass up. Raphael told me that George hadn't been to not one of his GED classes I signed them up for, and they had a test day scheduled. George felt like that shit was easy, and the classes were bullshit.

So, look, as a recruiter, I would get points for the type of people I put in. "Grad Alpha" is the most common and worth like 3 points, I think, memory is fuzzy. A Grad Alpha is a high school graduate that scored higher than a 50 on the ASVAB, that's our target citizen. Then there's Grad Bravo, and then Other. Other was GED holders, they aren't worth shit, and depending on the needs of the Army, there's times when they wouldn't be qualified to join. An Other could be counted as an Alpha if they scored higher than a 50 on the ASVAB and they passed this personality test.

So, George, George wasn't even an "other", he was less than an other, and he scored less than a 50 on the ASVAB. He wasn't worth shit to the Army. My station commander was telling me to just take the DEP loss and make it up, stop wasting my time with this punk that didn't even count towards my "Mission"(read: quota).

I did keep pushing him though though, I don't know why.

I personally drove this bastard to the GED test.

So, two weeks pass, and I pull his GED scores. Mother fucker failed the math portion. His ship out date was in 3 weeks. He needed to have his GED in his packet to ship out. Schedule him to retake the math portion the next week. Results only take 2 weeks to come back... if you know people.

He retakes the math portion. 2 weeks pass. His ship out date is tomorrow. His results aren't in....

So... I make it happen. I pull up someone else's passing GED, my own, and swap the names around. George now had a GED certificate in his packet. I pick him up and tell him that his results came in, he passed. I didn't even know if this dude passed. He shipped out on time though.

His results eventually did come in. He passed.

He kept in touch with me over the years. I was at his wedding, his baby shower, and he wasn't ever a stellar soldier, but I definitely made an impact for the better on his life.

I think that's what really matters. I put my career on the line to better the life of someone who was otherwise going no where. He wasn't the first or the last person that I lied for to get in the Army. I told him after basic that I forged his GED, but he actually did pass the test and the results came in after he left.

Next time on Recruiting Duty Blues: Dipping in the DEP Pool.

Edit: "but how were you a recruiter with only a GED?"

If you think I did shady shit in the Army, I personally did shady shit to join the Army. I was a Grad Alpha as far as the Army is concerned. Also, they don't do felony waivers for GED holders, you need a high school diploma or 15 college credits.

I didn't have a high school diploma or 15 credit hours. I'll tell you what I did have, a fucking printer.

Also, I shouldn't have ever been a recruiter with a felony record. I told them every day at recruiting school, "uhm, I don't think I'm supposed to be here, I have a felony record, and I can't be a recruiter." The Army is supposed to do background checks on people they assign to recruiting duty, but somehow, even with me telling them, I slipped through the cracks.
